did_you_know.text: Did you know? Amos opens the chapter with a lament over the house of Israel, describing the nation’s future condition as though it had already fallen and needed to be mourned.
Did you know? The phrase “Virgin Israel” is a poetic image for the people of Israel. In the verse, she is depicted as fallen on her land, with no one to raise her up.

Did you know? Amos conveys the scale of the destruction through numerical ratios: of a city from which a thousand go out, a hundred will remain; and of a city from which a hundred go out, ten will remain.
Did you know? At the heart of the warnings of destruction is a call to life: “Seek me and live.” According to the chapter, seeking the LORD is the way to be saved.
Did you know? Amos warns against turning to the worship centers at Bethel, Gilgal, and Beersheba. He presents Bethel as a place that will become nothing, and Gilgal as one that will go into exile.
Did you know? Amos describes the LORD as sovereign over creation: he made the Pleiades and Orion, turns day into night, calls for the waters of the sea, and pours them out over the earth.
Did you know? The city gate was a central place for administering justice, but the people described in the chapter hate those who rebuke them and reject those who speak the truth.
Did you know? Social injustice is evident in the way the rich exploit the poor. Therefore, although they build houses of hewn stone and plant vineyards, they will not enjoy the fruits of their labor.
Did you know? The moral climax of the chapter is the demand that justice roll on like water and righteousness like a never-failing stream—a picture of justice that is continuous, not a one-time act.
Did you know? Amos warns against a naïve expectation of the day of the LORD: for sinners, it will not be a day of light and salvation, but a day of darkness and judgment.
